## The idea

In D major, every written F means F-sharp unless a mark beside that note says
otherwise. The key signature establishes a persistent default. A natural sign
can override it for the rest of the bar, and the default returns at the next
barline.

A *key signature* maps letter names to sharp or flat alterations. An
*accidental* is a local override scoped to a bar and letter-octave position.
Notation behaves like nested configuration: global defaults, bar-local state,
and an explicit value on the current event. Reading becomes easier when those
layers are resolved in order.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}
key_signature = {f: 1, c: 1}  # D major

define :resolve_note do |event, key_signature, local, semitones|
  scope_key = [event[:letter], event[:octave]]
  local[scope_key] = event[:accidental] if event.key?(:accidental)
  alteration = local.fetch(scope_key, key_signature.fetch(event[:letter], 0))
  12 * (event[:octave] + 1) + semitones[event[:letter]] + alteration
end

bars = [
  [
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :g, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1, accidental: 0},
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1}
  ],
  [
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :c, octave: 5, duration: 1},
    {letter: :c, octave: 5, duration: 1, accidental: -1},
    {letter: :d, octave: 5, duration: 1}
  ]
]

bars.each do |bar|
  local = {}
  bar.each do |event|
    pitch = resolve_note(event, key_signature, local, semitones)
    puts "#{event} -> #{pitch}"
    play pitch, release: 0.7
    sleep event[:duration]
  end
end
```

The first F sounds sharp by default. The natural sign sets the local F4 override
to zero, so the next F4 in that bar remains natural. The local hash resets before
bar two, restoring F-sharp. C follows the same process with a flat override.

## Change one thing

1. Change the signature to `{b: -1, e: -1}` for B-flat major. The resolver needs
   no other change because flat and sharp alterations share one integer field.
2. Add F5 after the F4 natural. The local key includes octave, so F5 still uses
   the signature's F-sharp. Remove octave from `scope_key` and compare.
3. Put an explicit sharp after the natural within the same bar. The later
   accidental replaces the earlier local value, as a new assignment in scope.

## Why it works

The resolver searches from most local to most general. An accidental on the
event updates bar state. Existing bar state overrides the key signature. The key
signature overrides the natural pitch-class table. `fetch` makes those fallback
levels explicit.

Separating letter from alteration preserves spelling. F-sharp and G-flat can
produce the same MIDI number while retaining different letters and accidental
values. That distinction supports interval names, key logic, and faithful source
annotation.

Actual notation has further rules, including cancellation conventions and
accidentals tied across barlines. The small resolver covers the stated model and
keeps its limits visible. It should be extended from examples rather than grown
into a speculative notation engine.

Key signatures describe defaults by letter, which is why the circle-of-fifths
order matters again. D major sharpens F and C; it does not declare pitch classes
6 and 1 without names. A G-flat in the same piece has another spelling path even
when its MIDI value equals F-sharp. Preserve the source letter through resolution
so later diagnostics can distinguish an intended enharmonic choice from a typo.

## Take it further

Write `resolve_bar(events, key_signature)` that returns new event hashes with a
`:note` MIDI field while preserving letter, octave, start, duration, and
accidental data. Test it with a four-bar phrase containing one sharp signature,
one natural override, a repeated affected note, an octave-displaced note, and a
barline reset. Print source and resolved events side by side.
